questions.question: The chapter's epigraph is a parody about handing your data to a stranger over a laggy network. Who wrote it, and in what piece?

options.text: Kyle Kingsbury, Carly Rae Jepsen and the Perils of Network Partitions (2013)
Leslie Lamport, Time, Clocks and the Ordering of Events (1978)
Coda Hale, You Can't Sacrifice Partition Tolerance (2010)
Eric Brewer, CAP Twelve Years Later (2012)

questions.explanation: 'Hope' is the operative word — in an asynchronous network you cannot know whether the write landed.

questions.question: Which prior discussions does the opening name as examples of handling things going wrong? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Replica failover, under Handling Node Outages
Replication lag, under Problems with Replication Lag
Concurrency control for transactions, under Weak Isolation Levels
Schema evolution, under Modes of Dataflow

questions.explanation: As we come to understand various edge cases that can occur in real systems, we get better at handling them.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about the honesty of the previous chapters, and what assumption does it adopt?

options.text: Even though the book has talked a lot about faults, the last few chapters have still been too optimistic — the reality is even darker. The chapter now turns its pessimism to the maximum and assumes that anything that can go wrong will go wrong
The previous chapters were too pessimistic; this one assumes faults are rare
The previous chapters were accurate; this one adds only clock issues
The previous chapters ignored faults entirely

questions.explanation: A footnote carves out one exception: faults are assumed to be non-Byzantine, meaning nodes do not lie.

questions.question: What does the chapter name as the main difference between distributed systems and single-computer software?

options.text: That there are lots of new and exciting ways for things to go wrong
That performance is harder to predict
That the code is larger and harder to test
That data must be serialized

questions.explanation: The goal is a taste of the problems that arise in practice, and an understanding of the things we can and cannot rely on.

questions.question: How does the opening define the engineer's task?

options.text: To build systems that do their job — meet the guarantees users are expecting — in spite of everything going wrong. Chapter 9 gives examples of algorithms that can provide such guarantees, but first we need to understand what challenges we are up against
To eliminate all faults from the system
To detect faults as quickly as possible
To document all possible failure modes

questions.explanation: Guarantees despite faults, not absence of faults.

questions.question: Which problem areas does the opening preview, in order?

options.text: Unreliable networks (page 277); unreliable clocks and timing issues (page 287); and knowledge, truth, and lies (page 300)
Replication, partitioning and transactions
Consensus, ordering and atomic commit
Batch processing, stream processing and the future of data systems

questions.explanation: The chapter says the consequences of all these issues are disorienting, and describes itself as a thoroughly pessimistic and depressing overview of things that may go wrong, giving a bleak outlook.

questions.question: How does the chapter characterize a program running on a single computer?

options.text: It normally behaves in a fairly predictable way: either it works or it doesn't. Buggy software may give the appearance that the computer is 'having a bad day' — often fixed by a reboot — but that is mostly just a consequence of badly written software
It behaves unpredictably because of hardware variability
It behaves predictably only under low load
It always fails partially, like a distributed system

questions.explanation: There is no fundamental reason why software on a single computer should be flaky: when the hardware is working correctly, the same operation always produces the same result — it is deterministic.

questions.question: When a single computer does have a hardware problem, what is the usual consequence?

options.text: Usually total system failure — for example a kernel panic, a blue screen of death, or failure to start up. An individual computer with good software is usually either fully functional or entirely broken, but not something in between
Partial degradation with wrong results returned
Silent data corruption with no visible symptom
Reduced throughput but correct operation

questions.explanation: Examples given include a kernel panic, a blue screen of death, failure to start up, and memory corruption from a loose connector.

questions.question: Why is the all-or-nothing behaviour of a computer described as deliberate?

options.text: Because if an internal fault occurs we prefer a computer to crash completely rather than returning a wrong result, since wrong results are difficult and confusing to deal with — so computers deal with partial failure by letting it escalate into total failure
Because crashing is cheaper to implement than error recovery
Because operating systems cannot detect partial faults
It is not deliberate; it is an accident of hardware design

questions.explanation: Escalating partial failure into total failure is a design choice made to keep results trustworthy.

questions.question: What do computers hide, and how far back does the chapter trace this design goal?

options.text: They hide the fuzzy physical reality on which they are implemented and present an idealized system model that operates with mathematical perfection: a CPU instruction always does the same thing, and data written to memory or disk remains intact and doesn't get randomly corrupted. This design goal of always-correct computation goes all the way back to the very first digital computer
They hide network latency; the goal dates from the 1970s
They hide concurrency; the goal dates from the 1990s
They hide nothing; the physical reality is fully exposed

questions.explanation: The idealized model is what distributed systems cannot sustain.

questions.question: The Coda Hale anecdote lists failures from one operator's 'limited experience'. Which does it include? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Network partitions in a single datacenter, PDU failures and switch failures
Accidental power cycles of whole racks, whole-datacenter backbone failures and whole-datacenter power failures
A hypoglycemic driver smashing his Ford pickup truck into a datacenter's HVAC system
A software bug in the database engine

questions.explanation: And he adds 'I'm not even an ops guy' — in the physical world, a remarkably wide range of things can go wrong.

questions.question: Define partial failure, and say what makes it difficult.

options.text: In a distributed system there may well be some parts of the system that are broken in some unpredictable way, even though other parts of the system are working fine — this is known as a partial failure. The difficulty is that partial failures are nondeterministic: if you try to do anything involving multiple nodes and the network, it may sometimes work and sometimes unpredictably fail, and you may not even know whether something succeeded or not, as the time it takes for a message to travel across a network is also nondeterministic
Partial failure means half the nodes are down; the difficulty is capacity
Partial failure means data is partially written; the difficulty is corruption
Partial failure means slow responses; the difficulty is latency

questions.explanation: This nondeterminism and possibility of partial failures is what makes distributed systems hard to work with.

questions.question: Match the philosophies in the 'Cloud Computing and Supercomputing' box. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: High-performance computing: supercomputers with thousands of CPUs, typically used for computationally intensive scientific computing tasks such as weather forecasting or molecular dynamics
Cloud computing: often associated with multi-tenant datacenters, commodity computers connected with an IP network (often Ethernet), elastic/on-demand resource allocation, and metered billing
Traditional enterprise datacenters lie somewhere between these extremes
Cloud computing is a precisely defined technical term

questions.explanation: Note the honesty of the middle definition: cloud computing is not a well-defined term, so the chapter describes it by association.

questions.question: How does a supercomputer handle a fault?

options.text: A job typically checkpoints the state of its computation to durable storage from time to time; if one node fails, a common solution is to simply stop the entire cluster workload, repair the faulty node, and then restart the computation from the last checkpoint. Thus a supercomputer is more like a single-node computer than a distributed system: it deals with partial failure by letting it escalate into total failure, like a kernel panic on a single machine
It routes around the failed node automatically with no interruption
It replicates all state, so no checkpoint is needed
It ignores the failure and continues with degraded results

questions.explanation: The supercomputer model is deliberately the opposite of the cloud model.

questions.question: State the online/offline contrast between internet services and supercomputers.

options.text: Many internet-related applications are online, in the sense that they need to be able to serve users with low latency at any time, so making the service unavailable — for example stopping the cluster for repair — is not acceptable. In contrast, offline batch jobs like weather simulations can be stopped and restarted with fairly low impact
Both are online and cannot tolerate downtime
Both are offline and can be restarted freely
Internet services are offline; supercomputers are online

questions.explanation: Availability requirements are what rule out stop-and-repair for internet services.

questions.question: Contrast supercomputer and cloud nodes on hardware and communication.

options.text: Supercomputers are typically built from specialized hardware where each node is quite reliable, and nodes communicate through shared memory and remote direct memory access (RDMA). Nodes in cloud services are built from commodity machines, which can provide equivalent performance at lower cost due to economies of scale, but also have higher failure rates
Both use commodity hardware and message passing
Both use specialized hardware and shared memory
Supercomputers use commodity hardware; cloud uses specialized hardware

questions.explanation: Reliable specialized nodes with shared memory versus unreliable commodity nodes with messages.

questions.question: Which network topologies does the chapter attribute to each, and why?

options.text: Large datacenter networks are often based on IP and Ethernet, arranged in Clos topologies to provide high bisection bandwidth. Supercomputers commonly use specialized network topologies such as multi-dimensional meshes and toruses, which yield better performance for HPC workloads with known communication patterns
Both use Clos topologies for bisection bandwidth
Both use meshes and toruses for known communication patterns
Datacenters use toruses; supercomputers use Ethernet

questions.explanation: Known communication patterns is what makes a specialized topology pay for HPC.

questions.question: What does scale do to the probability of brokenness, and what does that cost the give-up-and-restart strategy?

options.text: The bigger a system gets, the more likely it is that one of its components is broken — over time, broken things get fixed and new things break, but in a system with thousands of nodes it is reasonable to assume that something is always broken. So when the error handling strategy consists of simply giving up, a large system can end up spending a lot of its time recovering from faults rather than doing useful work
Scale reduces the probability of brokenness through redundancy
Scale has no effect on brokenness
Scale makes give-up-and-restart cheaper

questions.explanation: 'Something is always broken' is the working assumption at scale.

questions.question: What operational benefits follow from tolerating failed nodes? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Rolling upgrade: restarting one node at a time, while the service continues serving users without interruption
In a cloud environment, if one virtual machine is not performing well, you can just kill it and request a new one, hoping that the new one will be faster
Faults become impossible
Checkpointing becomes unnecessary because state is never lost

questions.explanation: Both convert node-level disposability into operational freedom.

questions.question: Why does geographic distribution make things worse?

options.text: Because in a geographically distributed deployment — keeping data geographically close to users to reduce access latency — communication most likely goes over the internet, which is slow and unreliable compared to local networks. Supercomputers generally assume that all of their nodes are close together
Because clocks cannot be synchronized across distance
Because data cannot be replicated across regions
It does not make things worse

questions.explanation: The internet as the interconnect is the qualitative change.

questions.question: State the chapter's mandate for making distributed systems work, and its caveat.

options.text: If we want to make distributed systems work, we must accept the possibility of partial failure and build fault-tolerance mechanisms into the software — in other words, we need to build a reliable system from unreliable components. The caveat: there is no such thing as perfect reliability, so we'll need to understand the limits of what we can realistically promise
We must eliminate partial failure through better hardware
We must accept that distributed systems cannot be reliable
We must use supercomputer-style checkpointing

questions.explanation: Reliability from unreliability, with an honest ceiling.

questions.question: Why must even a small system think about partial failure? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Because it is important to consider a wide range of possible faults — even fairly unlikely ones — and to artificially create such situations in your testing environment to see what happens; in distributed systems, suspicion, pessimism, and paranoia pay off

Because in a distributed system, even if most of the components are working correctly most of the time, sooner or later some part of the system will become faulty, so fault handling must be part of the software design
Because you, as operator of the software, need to know what behavior to expect from the software in the case of a fault
Because it is wise to assume that faults are rare and simply hope for the best

questions.explanation: The last statement is exactly what the chapter says is unwise.

questions.question: The 'Building a Reliable System from Unreliable Components' box names an intuition and rejects it. Which?

options.text: That a system can only be as reliable as its least reliable component — its weakest link. This is not the case: in fact it is an old idea in computing to construct a more reliable system from a less reliable underlying base
That redundancy always improves reliability
That reliability is proportional to cost
That software can never be more reliable than hardware

questions.explanation: The whole box exists to contradict the weakest-link intuition.

questions.question: Which unreliability does each box example mask, and what are their limits? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Error-correcting codes allow digital data to be transmitted accurately across a communication channel that occasionally gets some bits wrong, for example due to radio interference on a wireless network

IP is unreliable — it may drop, delay, duplicate, or reorder packets — but TCP provides a more reliable transport layer on top: missing packets are retransmitted, duplicates are eliminated, and packets are reassembled into the order in which they were sent

Error correction can handle a small number of single-bit errors, but if your signal is swamped by interference there is a fundamental limit to how much data you can get through your communication channel
TCP can hide packet loss, duplication and reordering, but it cannot magically remove delays in the network

questions.explanation: Note which of IP's four sins TCP does not fix: delay. That omission is the seed of the entire unreliable-networks discussion.

questions.question: If the higher-level system is not perfect, why bother with a leaky abstraction?

options.text: Because it takes care of some of the tricky low-level faults, so the remaining faults are usually easier to reason about and deal with — the end-to-end argument explores this further
Because a leaky abstraction is always better than none
Because the abstraction can be made perfect with enough effort
You shouldn't bother; leaky abstractions should be removed

questions.explanation: Fewer and simpler remaining faults is the payoff, not their elimination.

questions.question: What kind of systems does Part II focus on, and what does the architecture forbid?

options.text: Shared-nothing systems: a bunch of machines connected by a network, which is the only way those machines can communicate. Each machine has its own memory and disk, and one machine cannot access another machine's memory or disk except by making requests to a service over the network — contrasting with supercomputers, which communicate through shared memory and remote direct memory access
Shared-disk systems, where all machines access one storage array
Shared-memory systems, using RDMA
Single-machine systems only

questions.explanation: Shared-nothing became dominant for internet services because it is comparatively cheap, requiring no special hardware; it can make use of commoditized cloud computing services; and it can achieve high reliability through redundancy across multiple geographically distributed datacenters.

questions.question: Define an asynchronous packet network.

options.text: The internet and most internal networks in datacenters, including Ethernet, are asynchronous packet networks: one node can send a message — a packet — to another node, but the network gives no guarantees as to when it will arrive, or whether it will arrive at all
A network with bounded delay and guaranteed delivery
A network where messages are delivered in order
A circuit-switched network with reserved bandwidth

questions.explanation: No timing guarantee and no delivery guarantee — both matter.

questions.question: You send a request and expect a response. Which failures are possible? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Your request may have been lost, perhaps someone unplugged a network cable; or it may be waiting in a queue and will be delivered later, perhaps the network or the recipient is overloaded

The remote node may have failed, perhaps it crashed or was powered down; or it may have temporarily stopped responding, perhaps because of a long garbage collection pause, but will start responding again later
The remote node may have processed your request, but the response has been lost on the network, perhaps a network switch has been misconfigured
The remote node may have processed your request, but the response has been delayed and will be delivered later, perhaps the network or your own machine is overloaded

questions.explanation: Six possibilities. Note the last one includes your own machine as a possible cause.

questions.question: Why can't the sender simply check whether its packet was delivered?

options.text: Because the sender can't even tell whether the packet was delivered: the only option is for the recipient to send a response message, which may in turn be lost or delayed. These issues are indistinguishable in an asynchronous network — the only information you have is that you haven't received a response yet, and it's impossible to tell why
Because the network protocol does not support acknowledgments
Because the sender's clock may be wrong
It can — TCP acknowledgments provide this

questions.explanation: Figure 8-1 shows that if you send a request and don't get a response, it's not possible to distinguish whether the request was lost, the remote node is down, or the response was lost.

questions.question: What does a timeout tell you, and what residual uncertainty remains?

options.text: After some time you give up waiting and assume that the response is not going to arrive. But even when a timeout expires you still don't know whether the remote node got your request or not — and if the request is still queued somewhere, it may still be delivered to the recipient even if the sender has given up on it
It tells you definitively that the node is dead
It tells you the request was not processed
It tells you the response was lost

questions.explanation: A timeout is a decision, not information.

questions.question: What did the study of a medium-sized datacenter find?

options.text: About 12 network faults per month, of which half disconnected a single machine and half disconnected an entire rack — so roughly 6 single-machine and 6 rack-level faults per month, around 0.4 faults per day or one every 2 to 3 days
About 2 network faults per year, all rack-level
About 100 faults per month, all single-machine
No network faults were observed

questions.explanation: 12 per month is roughly 144 per year, split 72/72 between single-machine and rack-level.

questions.question: Does redundant networking gear help as much as you might hope?

options.text: No — a study measuring the failure rates of components like top-of-rack switches, aggregation switches and load balancers found that adding redundant networking gear doesn't reduce faults as much as you might hope, since it doesn't guard against human error such as misconfigured switches, which is a major cause of outages
Yes, redundancy eliminates network faults entirely
Yes, redundancy reduces faults proportionally to the number of paths
The study found redundancy increases faults

questions.explanation: Human error is the failure mode redundancy does not address.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about public cloud versus private datacenter networks?

options.text: Public cloud services such as EC2 are notorious for having frequent transient network glitches, and well-managed private datacenter networks can be stabler environments — but nevertheless, nobody is immune from network problems
Private datacenters have no network faults
EC2 is more reliable than private datacenters
Both are equally unreliable with no difference

questions.explanation: A real difference in degree, but not in kind.

questions.question: What surprising fault involving a network interface does the chapter describe?

options.text: A network interface that sometimes drops all inbound packets but sends outbound packets successfully — the general lesson being that just because a network link works in one direction doesn't guarantee it's also working in the opposite direction
An interface that duplicates every packet it sends
An interface that reorders packets but never drops them
An interface that corrupts only inbound packets

questions.explanation: Asymmetric connectivity is what makes failure detection especially treacherous — picked up again under The Truth Is Defined by the Majority. The chapter also notes that sharks might bite undersea cables and damage them.

questions.question: What terminology does the 'Network partitions' box settle on, and why?

options.text: When one part of the network is cut off from the rest due to a network fault, that is sometimes called a network partition or netsplit. The book generally sticks with the more general term network fault, to avoid confusion with partitions (shards) of a storage system
It prefers 'netsplit' to avoid confusion with CAP
It prefers 'network partition' as the standard term
It uses all three terms interchangeably

questions.explanation: Avoiding collision with Chapter 6's sense of 'partition' is the reason.

questions.question: Which disasters does the chapter name for software meeting an untested network fault? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The cluster could become deadlocked and permanently unable to serve requests, even when the network recovers
It could delete all of your data
It could silently corrupt only recent writes
It could duplicate every write exactly once

questions.explanation: If software is put in an unanticipated situation it may do arbitrary unexpected things. The second example is cited from an analysis of Redis Sentinel properties and failure scenarios.

questions.question: Distinguish handling network faults from tolerating them.

options.text: Handling network faults doesn't necessarily mean tolerating them: if your network is normally fairly reliable, a valid approach may be to simply show an error message to users while the network is experiencing problems. But you do need to know how your software reacts to network problems and ensure that the system can recover from them — and it may make sense to deliberately trigger network problems and test the system's response, which is the idea behind Chaos Monkey
They are the same thing
Tolerating means showing an error; handling means recovering
Neither is necessary if the network is reliable

questions.explanation: Knowing the reaction is mandatory; masking the fault is optional.

questions.question: Why is automatic detection of faulty nodes needed? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A load balancer needs to stop sending requests to a node that is dead — take it out of rotation
In a distributed database with single-leader replication, if the leader fails, one of the followers needs to be promoted to be the new leader
To recompute the replication log from scratch
To synchronize clocks across the cluster

questions.explanation: Both require a verdict on liveness, which the network cannot supply reliably.

questions.question: What explicit feedback do you get when no process is listening on the destination port, and what does it fail to tell you?

options.text: The operating system will helpfully close or refuse the TCP connection by sending a RST or FIN packet in reply. But if the node crashed while it was handling your request, you have no way of knowing how much data was actually processed by the remote node
You get an ICMP echo reply confirming processing
You get nothing at all
You get a full transaction log of what was processed

questions.explanation: Connection-level feedback says nothing about application-level progress. A second mechanism: if a node process crashed but the operating system is still running, a script can notify other nodes about the crash so another node can take over without waiting for a timeout to expire — HBase does this.

questions.question: You can query switch management interfaces to detect link failures. When is that option ruled out? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If you're connecting via the internet
If you're in a shared datacenter with no access to the switches themselves
If you can't reach the management interface due to a network problem
If the remote machine is powered down

questions.explanation: The last case is subtle: hardware-level link detection rules out network faults but cannot distinguish a crash from a power-down that also killed the link.

questions.question: What does a router send when it is sure an address is unreachable, and what limitation applies?

options.text: It may reply with an ICMP Destination Unreachable packet — but the router doesn't have a magic failure detection capability either: it is subject to the same limitations as other participants of the network
An ICMP echo request, which is fully reliable
A TCP RST, which is definitive
Nothing; routers never report unreachability

questions.explanation: The router's knowledge is as partial as anyone else's.

questions.question: What is the chapter's rule about knowing a request succeeded?

options.text: You need a positive response from the application itself — even though TCP acknowledges that a packet was delivered, the application may have crashed before handling it
A TCP acknowledgment is sufficient
An absence of error is sufficient
A timeout not expiring is sufficient

questions.explanation: Rapid feedback about a remote node being down is useful but you can't count on it. The general procedure: you may get an error response at some level of the stack, but in general you have to assume that you will get no response at all — you can retry a few times, wait for a timeout to elapse, and eventually declare the node dead.

questions.question: How long should a timeout be? State the trade-off.

options.text: There is unfortunately no simple answer. A long timeout means a long wait until a node is declared dead, during which time users may have to wait or see error messages. A short timeout detects faults faster but carries a higher risk of incorrectly declaring a node dead when in fact it has only suffered a temporary slowdown, for example due to a load spike
Always use 30 seconds, the standard value
Always use the shortest possible timeout
Always use the longest tolerable timeout

questions.explanation: Detection latency versus false positives, with no universally right point.

questions.question: Why is prematurely declaring a node dead problematic?

options.text: Because the node may actually be alive and in the middle of performing some action — for example sending an email — and if another node takes over, the action may end up being performed twice
Because the node's data will be deleted
Because the node cannot rejoin the cluster
Because the clocks will drift further apart

questions.explanation: Duplicated side effects are the concrete harm; the chapter points forward to Chapters 9 and 11.

questions.question: Explain the cascading failure mechanism from premature timeouts.

options.text: When a node is declared dead, its responsibilities need to be transferred to other nodes, which places additional load on those nodes and on the network. If the system is already struggling with high load, declaring nodes dead prematurely can make the problem worse — in particular, it could happen that the node actually wasn't dead but only slow to respond due to overload, and transferring its load to other nodes can cause a cascading failure in the extreme case, where all nodes declare each other dead and everything stops working
Premature timeouts reduce load by shedding work
Premature timeouts only affect the timed-out node
Cascading failure is caused by long timeouts, not short ones

questions.explanation: Load transfer under overload is a positive feedback loop.

questions.question: In the fictitious system with bounded delays, what timeout follows — and for d = 20 ms and r = 100 ms, what is it?

options.text: Assuming packets are either delivered within some time d or lost (never taking longer than d), and that a nonfailed node always handles a request within some time r, every successful request receives a response within time 2d + r — so if you don't get a response within that time, either the network or the remote node is not working, making 2d + r a reasonable timeout. For d = 20 ms and r = 100 ms that gives 140 ms: a response at 125 ms is within budget and tells you nothing is wrong, while nothing by 145 ms means the timeout has fired
d + r, which is 120 ms
2(d + r), which is 240 ms
d + 2r, which is 220 ms

questions.explanation: Two network traversals plus one handling time.

questions.question: Why is 2d + r unavailable in reality?

options.text: Both assumptions fail. Asynchronous networks have unbounded delays — most network implementations try to deliver packets as quickly as possible, but there is no upper limit on the time it may take for a packet to arrive. And most server implementations cannot guarantee that they can handle requests within some maximum time; moreover, it is not sufficient for the system to be fast most of the time, since if your timeout is low, it only takes a transient spike in round-trip times to throw the system off-balance
Only the network assumption fails; response times are bounded
Only the response-time assumption fails; networks are bounded
Neither fails; 2d + r is used in practice

questions.explanation: Unbounded on both axes, and 'fast most of the time' is not the same as bounded.

questions.question: What analogy opens 'Network congestion and queueing', and what is the dominant cause of packet-delay variability?

options.text: The analogy is that travel times on road networks often vary most due to traffic congestion; similarly, variability of packet delays on computer networks is most often due to queueing
The analogy is air traffic control; the cause is routing changes
The analogy is postal delivery; the cause is packet loss
The analogy is water pipes; the cause is bandwidth limits

questions.explanation: Queueing, not distance or bandwidth, dominates delay variability.

questions.question: Which sources of queueing does the chapter list? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: At the network switch: if several different nodes simultaneously try to send packets to the same destination, the switch must queue them up and feed them into the destination network link one by one, so a packet may have to wait a while until it can get a slot — this is network congestion. If the switch queue fills up, the packet is dropped, so it has to be resent even though the network is functioning fine

At the destination machine: when a packet reaches the destination machine, if all CPU cores are currently busy, the incoming request from the network is queued by the operating system until the application is ready to handle it, which may take an arbitrary length of time

In virtualized environments: a running operating system is often paused for tens of milliseconds while another virtual machine uses a CPU core. During this time the VM cannot consume any data from the network, so incoming data is queued (buffered) by the virtual machine monitor, further increasing the variability of network delays

At the sender: TCP performs flow control, also known as congestion avoidance or backpressure, in which a node limits its own rate of sending in order to avoid overloading a network link or the receiving node — meaning additional queueing at the sender before the data even enters the network

questions.explanation: Four sources, at the switch, the destination CPU, the hypervisor and the sender.

questions.question: How does TCP decide a packet is lost, and what does the application observe?

options.text: TCP considers a packet to be lost if it is not acknowledged within some timeout, which is calculated from observed round-trip times, and lost packets are automatically retransmitted. Although the application does not see the packet loss and retransmission, it does see the resulting delay — the wait for the timeout to expire, and then the wait for the retransmitted packet to be acknowledged
TCP never retransmits; the application must handle loss
The application sees the loss but not the delay
TCP retransmits immediately with no timeout

questions.explanation: Two waits, serially — which is exactly the delay TCP cannot magically remove.

questions.question: What does the 'TCP Versus UDP' box say about UDP?

options.text: Some latency-sensitive applications such as videoconferencing and Voice over IP use UDP rather than TCP: it's a trade-off between reliability and variability of delays, since UDP does not perform flow control and does not retransmit lost packets — but it is still susceptible to switch queues and scheduling delays, so it does not escape delay variability
UDP eliminates all delay variability
UDP performs flow control but not retransmission
UDP is more reliable than TCP

questions.explanation: Dropping reliability reduces some sources of delay but not queueing or scheduling.

questions.question: Why is retransmission pointless in a VoIP call?

options.text: Because in situations where delayed data is worthless there is no point retransmitting: in a VoIP phone call there probably isn't enough time to retransmit a lost packet before its data is due to be played over the loudspeakers, so the application must instead fill the missing packet's time slot with silence — causing a brief interruption in the sound — and move on in the stream. The retry happens at the human layer instead: 'could you repeat that please? The sound just cut out for a moment'
Because UDP forbids retransmission at the protocol level
Because audio packets are too large to retransmit
Because voice data is not error-sensitive

questions.explanation: The deadline, not the protocol, is what makes retransmission worthless.

questions.question: Why do queueing delays have an especially wide range near maximum capacity?

options.text: Because a system with plenty of spare capacity can easily drain queues, whereas in a highly utilized system long queues can build up very quickly
Because switches drop more packets at low utilization
Because TCP disables flow control near capacity
Because CPU scheduling becomes deterministic near capacity

questions.explanation: Queue growth is nonlinear in utilization, which is why tail latency explodes near saturation.

questions.question: In multi-tenant environments, what is shared and what term describes the offender?

options.text: You have no control over or insight into other customers' usage of the shared resources: the network links and switches, and even each machine's network interface and CPUs when running on virtual machines. Network delays can be highly variable if someone near you — a noisy neighbor — is using a lot of resources, and batch workloads such as MapReduce can easily saturate network links
Only network links are shared; the term is congestion
Only CPUs are shared; the term is steal time
Nothing is shared in multi-tenant environments

questions.explanation: Links, switches, interfaces and CPUs all shared — hence unpredictable delays.

questions.question: What measurement procedure does the chapter prescribe for choosing timeouts?

options.text: Rather than using configured constant timeouts, measure the distribution of network round-trip times over an extended period and over many machines to determine the expected variability of delays; then, taking into account your application's characteristics, you can determine an appropriate trade-off between failure detection delay and risk of premature timeouts
Use the maximum observed round-trip time from a single machine
Use the vendor's recommended default
Use the p50 of a one-minute sample

questions.explanation: Measured distribution, not a guessed constant.

questions.question: What does the chapter recommend instead of constant timeouts, and which systems use it?

options.text: Systems can continually measure response times and their variability (jitter) and automatically adjust timeouts according to the observed response time distribution — this can be done with a Phi Accrual failure detector, which is used in Akka and Cassandra; TCP retransmission timeouts also work similarly
A fixed exponential backoff, used in HBase and Kafka
A fixed 30-second timeout, used in ZooKeeper
No timeout at all, used in Riak

questions.explanation: Adaptive timeouts driven by measured jitter.

questions.question: Which comparison case does the chapter reach for when asking why networks can't just be made reliable?

options.text: The traditional fixed-line telephone network — non-cellular, non-VoIP — which is extremely reliable: delayed audio frames and dropped calls are very rare. It requires a constantly low end-to-end latency and enough bandwidth to transfer the audio samples of your voice
The postal system, which guarantees delivery
The electrical grid, which guarantees voltage
The air traffic control network

questions.explanation: A network that does deliver bounded latency, which invites the question of why datacenters can't.

questions.question: Describe a telephone circuit and the ISDN numbers.

options.text: When you make a call over the telephone network it establishes a circuit: a fixed, guaranteed amount of bandwidth is allocated for the call along the entire route between the two callers, and this circuit remains in place until the call ends. An ISDN network runs at a fixed rate of 4,000 frames per second, and when a call is established it is allocated 16 bits of space within each frame in each direction — so for the duration of the call, each side is guaranteed to be able to send exactly 16 bits of audio data every 250 microseconds, which works out to 64,000 bits per second
8,000 frames per second with 8 bits each, giving 64,000 bits per second
4,000 frames per second with 8 bits each, giving 32,000 bits per second
1,000 frames per second with 64 bits each

questions.explanation: 4,000 frames per second is one frame every 250 microseconds; 4,000 times 16 bits is 64,000 bits per second.

questions.question: Why does a circuit give bounded delay?

options.text: Because this kind of network is synchronous: even as data passes through several routers, it does not suffer from queueing, since the 16 bits of space for the call have already been reserved in the next hop of the network — and because there is no queueing, the maximum end-to-end latency of the network is fixed, giving a bounded delay
Because the routers are faster than packet routers
Because the circuit uses UDP instead of TCP
Because the data volume is small

questions.explanation: Pre-reserved capacity at every hop is what eliminates queueing.

questions.question: Contrast a telephone circuit with a TCP connection.

options.text: A circuit is a fixed amount of reserved bandwidth which nobody else can use while the circuit is established, whereas the packets of a TCP connection opportunistically use whatever network bandwidth is available. You can give TCP a variable-sized block of data and it will try to transfer it in the shortest time possible; while a TCP connection is idle it doesn't use any bandwidth — a footnote adds, except for an occasional keepalive packet if TCP keepalive is enabled
Both reserve bandwidth; TCP simply reserves less
Both are opportunistic; the circuit merely has priority
A TCP connection reserves bandwidth while idle

questions.explanation: Reservation versus opportunism is the whole difference.

questions.question: Why can't Ethernet and IP promise a maximum round-trip time?

options.text: Because Ethernet and IP are packet-switched protocols, which suffer from queueing and thus unbounded delays in the network — these protocols do not have the concept of a circuit
Because Ethernet is too slow
Because IP is stateless
They can, but implementations choose not to

questions.explanation: No circuit means no reservation means queueing means unbounded delay.

questions.question: Which hybrid attempts does the chapter cite, and what does InfiniBand do?

options.text: Hybrids such as ATM. InfiniBand has some similarities: it implements end-to-end flow control at the link layer, which reduces the need for queueing in the network, although it can still suffer from delays due to link congestion. A footnote notes that Asynchronous Transfer Mode was a competitor to Ethernet in the 1980s but didn't gain much adoption outside of telephone network core switches, has nothing to do with automatic teller machines, and speculates that in some parallel universe where the internet is based on something like ATM, internet video calls are probably a lot more reliable
Only MPLS; InfiniBand is a storage protocol
Only Token Ring; InfiniBand implements circuit switching
No hybrids exist

questions.explanation: Link-layer flow control reduces but does not eliminate queueing.

questions.question: How can circuits be emulated on packet networks?

options.text: With quality of service (QoS), meaning prioritization and scheduling of packets, and admission control (rate-limiting senders) — which together make it possible to emulate circuit switching on packet networks, or to provide statistically bounded delay
By disabling TCP flow control
By reserving IP addresses per flow
Circuits cannot be emulated on packet networks

questions.explanation: Note 'statistically bounded' — not the same as bounded.

questions.question: Work through the 'Latency and Resource Utilization' box's 10,000-call wire example.

options.text: If the maximum number of simultaneous calls in a circuit-switched network is fixed, each call occupies one of those call slots for its duration — it's a kind of static resource partitioning. But that allocation is wasteful: if yours is the only call on the wire right now, all other 9,999 slots are unused, and your call is still allocated the same fixed amount of bandwidth as when the wire is fully utilized. You get a guarantee of latency, but only 0.01% of capacity is in use and 99.99% is idle. The general principle: you can think of variable delays as a consequence of dynamic resource partitioning
All 10,000 slots are shared dynamically, giving no guarantee
The wire adapts its capacity to the number of calls
Unused slots are reallocated to active calls

questions.explanation: Static partitioning buys guarantees and wastes capacity.

questions.question: How does the internet allocate bandwidth, and what is the upside of the resulting queueing?

options.text: It shares network bandwidth dynamically: senders push and jostle with each other to get their packets over the wire as quickly as possible, and the network switches decide which packet to send from one moment to the next. This approach has the downside of queueing, but the advantage is that it maximizes utilization of the wire — the wire has a fixed cost, so if you utilize it better, each byte you send over the wire is cheaper
It reserves bandwidth per flow, with no queueing and no cost benefit
It allocates round-robin, giving bounded delay
It does not allocate bandwidth at all

questions.explanation: Cheaper bytes is the payoff for accepting variable delay.

questions.question: How does the box carry the argument over to CPUs?

options.text: A similar situation arises with CPUs: if you share each CPU core dynamically between several threads, one thread sometimes has to wait in the operating system's run queue while another thread is running, so a thread can be paused for varying lengths of time — but this utilizes the hardware better than if you allocated a static number of CPU cycles to each thread. Better hardware utilization is also a significant motivation for using virtual machines
CPUs are always statically partitioned, unlike networks
CPU scheduling has no effect on latency
The argument does not carry over to CPUs

questions.explanation: The same utilization-versus-predictability trade-off, one layer down.

questions.question: State the box's closing verdict.

options.text: Latency guarantees are achievable in certain environments if resources are statically partitioned — as in dedicated hardware and exclusive bandwidth allocations — but it comes at the cost of reduced utilization, and is therefore more expensive. On the other hand, multi-tenancy with dynamic resource partitioning provides better utilization, so it is cheaper, but it has the downside of variable delays. Variable delays in networks are not a law of nature, but simply the result of a cost/benefit trade-off
Variable delays are a law of nature and cannot be avoided
Static partitioning is always cheaper
Dynamic partitioning gives both low cost and bounded delay

questions.explanation: 'Not a law of nature, but a cost/benefit trade-off' is the line to remember.

questions.question: Where does the chapter say quality of service is currently not enabled?

options.text: In multi-tenant datacenters and public clouds, or when communicating via the internet — so currently deployed technology does not allow us to make any guarantees about delays or reliability of the network: we have to assume that network congestion, queueing, and unbounded delays will happen. Consequently there's no 'correct' value for timeouts; they need to be determined experimentally
Only in private datacenters
Only on wireless networks
QoS is enabled everywhere by default

questions.explanation: A footnote notes that peering agreements between internet service providers and the establishment of routes through the Border Gateway Protocol bear closer resemblance to circuit switching than IP itself — at that level it is possible to buy dedicated bandwidth, but internet routing operates at the level of networks, not individual connections between hosts, and at a much longer timescale.

questions.question: True or false: an asynchronous network has bounded delay; a synchronous network avoids queueing because bandwidth is reserved at every hop; TCP turns an unbounded-delay network into a bounded-delay one; statistically bounded delay is the same as bounded delay.

options.text: False, true, false, false — asynchronous networks have unbounded delays with no upper limit; synchronous networks reserve space in the next hop so end-to-end latency is fixed; TCP cannot magically remove delays, hiding only loss, duplication and reordering; and QoS plus admission control gives statistically bounded delay, which is not a hard bound
True, true, true, true
False, false, true, true
True, false, false, true

questions.explanation: Only the synchronous-network claim is true as stated.

questions.question: Which questions does the chapter list that applications use clocks to answer? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Has this request timed out yet? What's the 99th percentile response time of this service?
How many queries per second did this service handle on average in the last five minutes? How long did the user spend on our site?
When was this article published? At what date and time should the reminder email be sent?
When does this cache entry expire? What is the timestamp on this error message in the log file?

questions.explanation: Eight questions in all: the first four measure durations, the last four describe points in time.

questions.question: What is the core reason time is tricky in a distributed system?

options.text: Because communication is not instantaneous: it takes time for a message to travel across the network from one machine to another, so the time when a message is received is always later than the time when it is sent — but due to variable delays in the network, we don't know how much later. This fact sometimes makes it difficult to determine the order in which things happened when multiple machines are involved
Because clocks are cheap and therefore inaccurate
Because time zones differ between machines
Because leap seconds are unpredictable

questions.explanation: Unknown, variable message delay is what breaks ordering by timestamp.

questions.question: What physical device is a machine's clock, and what is the standard synchronization mechanism?

options.text: Each machine on the network has its own clock, an actual hardware device — usually a quartz crystal oscillator. These devices are not perfectly accurate, so each machine has its own notion of time which may be slightly faster or slower than on other machines. It is possible to synchronize clocks to some degree: the most commonly used mechanism is the Network Time Protocol (NTP), which allows the computer clock to be adjusted according to the time reported by a group of servers, which in turn get their time from a more accurate time source such as a GPS receiver
An atomic clock, synchronized by GPS directly
A software counter, synchronized by the operating system
A network timestamp, with no local device

questions.explanation: Note it is a group of servers, which is what allows outlier rejection.

questions.question: Define the time-of-day clock precisely.

options.text: It returns the current date and time according to some calendar, also known as wall-clock time — for example clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME) on Linux and System.currentTimeMillis() in Java return the number of seconds or milliseconds since the epoch: midnight UTC on January 1, 1970, according to the Gregorian calendar, not counting leap seconds. Some systems use other dates as their reference point
It returns nanoseconds since the computer was started
It returns a monotonically increasing counter with no calendar meaning
It returns seconds since the year 2000 including leap seconds

questions.explanation: A footnote clarifies that although the clock is called real-time, it has nothing to do with real-time operating systems.

questions.question: Why can't time-of-day clocks measure elapsed time? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Backward jumps: if the local clock is too far ahead of the NTP server, it may be forcibly reset and appear to jump back to a previous point in time
Leap seconds: they often ignore leap seconds, which makes the timeline inconsistent
They have coarse-grained resolution — for example moving forward only in steps of 10 ms on older Windows systems
They cannot be synchronized at all

questions.explanation: The jumps and leap-second handling make them unsuitable for measuring elapsed time; the resolution problem is less of a problem on recent systems. Time-of-day clocks are usually synchronized with NTP, which means a timestamp from one machine ideally means the same as on another.

questions.question: Define the monotonic clock and explain its name.

options.text: A monotonic clock is suitable for measuring a duration or time interval, such as a timeout or a service's response time — for example clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) on Linux and System.nanoTime() in Java. The name comes from the fact that they are guaranteed to always move forward, whereas a time-of-day clock may jump back in time
It returns calendar time and is named for its monotone units
It is named for being monotonic in frequency, not in value
It always moves backward on resynchronization

questions.explanation: Guaranteed forward movement is precisely what the time-of-day clock lacks.

questions.question: How do you use a monotonic clock value, and what is forbidden?

options.text: You can check the value at one point in time, do something, then check the clock again at a later time: the difference between the two values tells you how much time elapsed between the two checks. But the absolute value of the clock is meaningless — it might be the number of nanoseconds since the computer was started, or something similarly arbitrary — so it makes no sense to compare monotonic clock values from two different computers, because they don't mean the same thing
You compare absolute values across machines to order events
You use the absolute value as a timestamp in stored data
You compare it against a time-of-day clock to detect drift

questions.explanation: Differences within a machine are meaningful; absolute values and cross-machine comparisons are not.

questions.question: What complication arises with multiple CPU sockets?

options.text: In a server with multiple CPU sockets there may be a separate timer per CPU, not necessarily synchronized with other CPUs. Operating systems compensate for any discrepancy and try to present a monotonic view of the clock to application threads even when they are scheduled across different CPUs — but it is wise to take this guarantee of monotonicity with a pinch of salt
There is one timer shared by all sockets, so no complication arises
The operating system exposes each socket's timer separately
Multi-socket servers cannot provide a monotonic clock at all

questions.explanation: The OS papers over it, imperfectly.

questions.question: What is slewing, and what can NTP do and not do to a monotonic clock?

options.text: NTP may adjust the frequency at which the monotonic clock moves forward — known as slewing the clock — if it detects that the computer's local quartz is moving faster or slower than the NTP server. By default NTP allows the clock rate to be speeded up or slowed down by up to 0.05%, but NTP cannot cause the monotonic clock to jump forward or backward. On most systems monotonic clocks can measure time intervals in microseconds or less
Slewing means jumping the clock; NTP can slew but not adjust frequency
NTP can jump the monotonic clock but not slew it
NTP cannot affect the monotonic clock at all

questions.explanation: 0.05% is 500 parts per million, which over an hour is about 1.8 seconds and over a day about 43.2 seconds.

questions.question: Why are monotonic clocks fine in distributed systems?

options.text: Because using a monotonic clock for measuring elapsed time such as timeouts is usually fine: it doesn't assume any synchronization between different nodes' clocks, and it is not sensitive to slight inaccuracies of measurement
Because they are synchronized by NTP across nodes
Because their absolute values are comparable
They are not fine; time-of-day clocks are preferred

questions.explanation: Monotonic clocks don't need synchronization, but time-of-day clocks need to be set according to an NTP server or other external time source in order to be useful.

questions.question: Which properties belong to the monotonic clock? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It is meaningless to compare its values across machines
It can be slewed but never jumped by NTP
It is the right tool for measuring a service's response time
It counts seconds since a calendar epoch

questions.explanation: Counting from a calendar epoch, jumping backward, needing an external time source, and being right for a 'when was this published' field all belong to the time-of-day clock.

questions.question: What is clock drift, what figure does Google assume, and what does it imply?

options.text: A clock is not very accurate: it drifts, running faster or slower than it should, depending among other things on the temperature of the machine. Google assumes a clock drift of 200 parts per million for its servers, which is equivalent to 6 ms drift for a clock that is resynchronized with a server every 30 seconds, or 17 seconds drift for a clock resynchronized once a day. This drift limits the best possible accuracy you can achieve, even if everything is working correctly
Google assumes 2 ppm, giving 0.06 ms over 30 seconds
Google assumes 2000 ppm, giving 60 ms over 30 seconds
Clock drift is constant per machine regardless of temperature

questions.explanation: At 200 ppm, an hour of drift is about 0.72 seconds and a week is about 121 seconds — roughly two minutes.

questions.question: What happens when a computer's clock differs too much from its NTP server?

options.text: It may refuse to synchronize, or the local clock will be forcibly reset — and if this happens, it can appear to applications observing the time before and after this reset that time went backward or suddenly jumped forward
It slews gradually with no visible jump
It raises an error to all applications
It shuts down the machine

questions.explanation: A node can also be accidentally firewalled off from NTP servers, and the misconfiguration may go unnoticed for some time — anecdotal evidence suggests this does happen in practice.

questions.question: How accurate can NTP be over the internet, and how does it fail?

options.text: NTP synchronization can only be as good as the network delay, so there is a limit to its accuracy on a congested network with variable packet delays. One experiment showed a minimum error of 35 ms when synchronizing over the internet, though occasional spikes in network delay lead to errors of around a second; and depending on configuration, large network delays can cause the NTP client to give up entirely
NTP is accurate to microseconds over the internet with no failure mode
NTP is accurate to 1 ms with spikes to 5 ms
NTP accuracy is independent of network delay

questions.explanation: The 35 ms minimum is about 350 times worse than the 100-microsecond MiFID II requirement, and the one-second spike is about 30 times worse again than the 35 ms floor.

questions.question: How wrong can NTP servers be, and why are clients nonetheless robust?

options.text: Some NTP servers are wrong or misconfigured, reporting time that is off by hours. NTP clients are quite robust because they query several servers and ignore outliers — but it's somewhat worrying to bet the correctness of your systems on the time that you were told by a stranger on the internet
NTP servers are never wrong; clients trust a single server
NTP servers can be off by milliseconds at most
Clients ignore all servers and use the local clock

questions.explanation: The NTP client contacts all configured servers, estimates their errors, and checks that a majority of servers agree on some time range — so a misconfigured server is detected as an outlier and excluded from synchronization.

questions.question: What happens to clocks in virtual machines?

options.text: The hardware clock is virtualized, which raises additional challenges for applications that need accurate timekeeping: when one CPU core is shared between virtual machines, each VM is paused for tens of milliseconds while another VM is running, and from an application's point of view this pause manifests itself as the clock suddenly jumping forward
Virtual machines have perfectly accurate clocks provided by the hypervisor
Virtual machine clocks run backward during pauses
Virtualization has no effect on clocks

questions.explanation: The same phenomenon as the hypervisor-induced network queueing, seen through the clock.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about clocks on devices you don't control?

options.text: If you run software on devices that you don't fully control — for example mobile or embedded devices — you probably cannot trust the device's hardware clock at all: some users deliberately set their hardware clock to an incorrect date and time, for instance to circumvent timing limitations in games, so the clock may be set wildly in the past or the future
Mobile device clocks are synchronized by the carrier and always correct
Embedded devices have atomic clocks
Users cannot change hardware clocks

questions.explanation: Deliberate manipulation is the specific risk, not just drift.

questions.question: State the MiFID II clock requirement and its purposes.

options.text: The draft European regulation for financial institutions requires all high-frequency trading funds to synchronize their clocks to within 100 microseconds of UTC, in order to help debug market anomalies such as 'flash crashes' and to help detect market manipulation. It is possible to achieve very good clock accuracy if you care about it sufficiently to invest significant resources
Within 100 milliseconds of UTC, to help with billing
Within 1 second of UTC, to help with audit logging
Within 1 microsecond of UTC, to help with order matching

questions.explanation: 100 microseconds is about 350 times tighter than the 35 ms minimum error seen when synchronizing over the internet, and about 70 times tighter than a few milliseconds on a local network.

questions.question: How is such accuracy achieved, and how does it break?

options.text: Through GPS receivers, the Precision Time Protocol (PTP), and careful deployment and monitoring — but it requires significant effort and expertise, and there are plenty of ways clock synchronization can go wrong: if your NTP daemon is misconfigured, or a firewall is blocking NTP traffic, the clock error due to drift can quickly become large
Through NTP alone, which never fails
Through atomic clocks in every machine, which cannot fail
It cannot be achieved at all

questions.explanation: Achievable but expensive, and fragile in operation.

questions.question: True or false: a drifting clock usually announces itself by failing loudly; NTP can be more accurate than the network round-trip time; a misconfigured NTP server reporting a time off by hours will typically be ignored by clients; clock drift is a constant per machine.

options.text: False, false, true, false — most things will seem to work fine with a defective quartz clock or misconfigured NTP client, making silent and subtle data loss more likely than a dramatic crash; NTP synchronization can only be as good as the network delay and is itself limited by the round-trip time; clients query several servers and exclude outliers; and clock drift varies depending on the temperature of the machine
True, true, true, true
False, true, false, true
True, false, true, false

questions.explanation: Only the outlier-rejection claim is true as stated.

questions.question: Why are broken clocks worse than broken CPUs?

options.text: If a node's CPU is defective or its network is misconfigured, it most likely won't work at all, so it will quickly be noticed and fixed — but if its quartz clock is defective or its NTP client is misconfigured, most things will seem to work fine even though its clock gradually drifts further and further away from reality. The result is likely to be silent and subtle data loss rather than a dramatic crash, and part of the problem is that incorrect clocks easily go unnoticed
Broken clocks crash the machine, unlike broken CPUs
Broken clocks are always detected by monitoring
They are equally noticeable

questions.explanation: Silence is the danger: the fault does not announce itself.

questions.question: If your software requires synchronized clocks, what is essential?

options.text: It is essential that you also carefully monitor the clock offsets between all the machines: any node whose clock drifts too far from the others should be declared dead and removed from the cluster. Such monitoring ensures that you notice the broken clocks before they can cause too much damage
It is essential to use only monotonic clocks
It is essential to disable NTP
No monitoring is needed if NTP is configured

questions.explanation: Treat a drifting clock as a node failure.

questions.question: Walk through Figure 8-3's sequence of events.

options.text: It illustrates a dangerous use of time-of-day clocks in a database with multi-leader replication, similar to Figure 5-9. Client A writes x = 1 on node 1, and the write is replicated to node 3; client B increments x on node 3, so we now have x = 2; and finally both writes are replicated to node 2. When a write is replicated to other nodes it is tagged with a timestamp according to the time-of-day clock on the node where the write originated
It shows single-leader replication with a failover
It shows leaderless replication with quorum reads
It shows a partitioned database with cross-partition writes

questions.explanation: Multi-leader plus timestamp-tagged writes is the dangerous combination.

questions.question: What are the timestamps and the ordering error in Figure 8-3?

options.text: The clock synchronization is very good in this example — the skew between node 1 and node 3 is less than 3 ms, probably better than you can expect in practice — yet the write x = 1 has a timestamp of 42.004 seconds while the write x = 2 has a timestamp of 42.003 seconds, even though x = 2 occurred unambiguously later. So the later write is stamped 1 ms earlier than the earlier one
The skew is 300 ms and the error is 100 ms
The timestamps are correctly ordered; there is no error
The skew is 3 seconds and the error is 1 second

questions.explanation: Very good synchronization still inverts the order of causally related writes.

questions.question: What does node 2 do, and what is the outcome?

options.text: The write by client B is causally later than the write by client A, but B's write has an earlier timestamp — so when node 2 receives these two events it will incorrectly conclude that x = 1 is the more recent value and drop the write x = 2. In effect, client B's increment operation will be lost, and no error is reported to anyone
Node 2 detects the inversion and raises an error
Node 2 keeps both values as siblings
Node 2 drops the write x = 1

questions.explanation: This is the last write wins conflict resolution strategy, widely used in both multi-leader replication and leaderless databases such as Cassandra and Riak. Some implementations generate timestamps on the client rather than the server, but this doesn't change the fundamental problems with LWW.

questions.question: Which problems does the chapter name with last write wins? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Database writes can mysteriously disappear: a node with a lagging clock is unable to overwrite values previously written by a node with a fast clock until the clock skew between the nodes has elapsed, allowing arbitrary amounts of data to be silently dropped without any error being reported to the application

LWW cannot distinguish between writes that occurred sequentially in quick succession — where client B's increment definitely occurs after client A's write — and writes that were truly concurrent, where neither writer was aware of the other. Additional causality tracking mechanisms such as version vectors are needed to prevent violations of causality

It is possible for two nodes to independently generate writes with the same timestamp, especially when the clock only has millisecond resolution; an additional tiebreaker value — which can simply be a large random number — is required to resolve such conflicts, but this approach can also lead to violations of causality
LWW causes disk corruption

questions.explanation: Three problems: vanishing writes, conflated sequential and concurrent writes, and timestamp collisions.

questions.question: What illustration does the chapter give of residual skew even under tight NTP synchronization?

options.text: It is possible to have two nodes with tightly NTP-synchronized clocks where node 1 sends a packet at timestamp 100 ms by its own clock and node 2 receives it at timestamp 99 ms by its clock — so it appears as though the packet arrived before it was sent, which is impossible. When picking the most 'recent' value and discarding others, it's important to be aware that the definition of 'recent' depends on a local time-of-day clock, which may well be incorrect
A packet arrives 100 ms after it was sent, which is expected
Two nodes report identical timestamps for different events
The clocks jump backward simultaneously

questions.explanation: An impossible ordering produced by a few milliseconds of residual skew.

questions.question: Could NTP be made accurate enough that incorrect orderings cannot occur?

options.text: Probably not, because NTP's synchronization accuracy is itself limited by the network round-trip time, in addition to other sources of error such as quartz drift — for correct ordering you would need the clock source to be significantly more accurate than the thing you are measuring, namely network delay
Yes, with GPS receivers NTP becomes exact
Yes, with sub-millisecond NTP on a local network
The question is meaningless

questions.explanation: The measuring instrument is bounded by the very quantity it must resolve.

questions.question: Define logical clocks and contrast them with physical clocks.

options.text: Logical clocks are based on incrementing counters rather than an oscillating quartz crystal, and are a safer alternative for ordering events. They do not measure the time of day or the number of seconds elapsed, only the relative ordering of events — whether one event happened before or after another. In contrast, time-of-day and monotonic clocks, which measure actual elapsed time, are also known as physical clocks
Logical clocks measure elapsed time more precisely than physical clocks
Logical clocks are synchronized by NTP
Logical and physical clocks are the same thing

questions.explanation: Ordering without magnitude is exactly what causality needs.

questions.question: Distinguish a clock's resolution from its accuracy, and give the accuracy figures.

options.text: Clocks can return fractional seconds with microsecond or even nanosecond resolution, but that doesn't mean the value is actually accurate to such precision — in fact it most likely is not. Even if you synchronize with an NTP server on the local network every minute, the quartz drift can easily be several milliseconds. With an NTP server on the public internet the best possible accuracy is probably to the tens of milliseconds, and the error may easily spike to over 100 ms when there is network congestion
Resolution equals accuracy in modern systems
Accuracy is always better than resolution
Accuracy on a local network is nanoseconds

questions.explanation: Fine resolution on an inaccurate reading is precision theatre.

questions.question: How do you compute the clock uncertainty bound? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If you have a GPS receiver or atomic (caesium) clock directly attached to your computer, the expected error range is reported by the manufacturer

If you're getting the time from a server, the uncertainty is based upon the expected quartz drift since your last sync with the server, plus the NTP server's own uncertainty, plus the network round-trip time to the server — to a first approximation, and assuming you trust the server
It equals the clock's resolution
It is always zero for synchronized clocks

questions.explanation: Most systems don't expose this uncertainty: when you ask for the time using clock_gettime() the return value doesn't tell you the expected error of the timestamp, so you don't know if its confidence interval is five milliseconds or five years.

questions.question: Describe Google's TrueTime API.

options.text: TrueTime in Spanner explicitly reports the confidence interval on the local clock: when you ask it for the current time you get back two values, [earliest, latest], being the earliest possible and the latest possible timestamp. Based on its uncertainty calculations the clock knows that the actual current time is somewhere within that interval, and the width of the interval depends among other things on how long it has been since the local quartz clock was last synchronized with a more accurate clock source
It returns a single exact timestamp guaranteed correct to the nanosecond
It returns a logical counter with no physical meaning
It returns the network round-trip time

questions.explanation: An interval rather than a point is the key design move.

questions.question: Why are distributed transaction IDs hard to generate? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Coordination: a global, monotonically increasing transaction ID across all partitions is difficult to generate, because it requires coordination

Causality: the transaction ID must reflect causality — if transaction B reads a value that was written by transaction A, then B must have a higher transaction ID than A, otherwise the snapshot would not be consistent
With lots of small, rapid transactions, creating transaction IDs in a distributed system becomes an untenable bottleneck
Because transaction IDs must be globally unique strings

questions.explanation: A footnote notes that distributed sequence number generators do exist, such as Twitter's Snowflake, which generate approximately monotonically increasing unique IDs in a scalable way by allocating blocks of the ID space to different nodes — but they typically cannot guarantee an ordering that is consistent with causality, because the timescale at which blocks of IDs are assigned is longer than the timescale of database reads and writes.

questions.question: State the observation Spanner's snapshot isolation is based on.

options.text: If you have two confidence intervals as reported by TrueTime, A = [A_earliest, A_latest] and B = [B_earliest, B_latest], and those two intervals do not overlap — that is, A_earliest is before A_latest, which is before B_earliest, which is before B_latest — then B definitely happened after A, there can be no doubt. Only if the intervals overlap are we unsure in which order A and B happened
If the midpoints of the intervals differ, the order is determined
If the intervals overlap, the order is determined by node ID
Interval comparison never determines order

questions.explanation: Non-overlap gives a provable order; overlap gives none.

questions.question: What does Spanner deliberately do before committing, and what hardware makes it affordable?

options.text: It deliberately waits for the length of the confidence interval before committing a read-write transaction, ensuring that any transaction that may read the data is at a sufficiently later time so their confidence intervals do not overlap. In order to keep the wait time as short as possible, Spanner needs to keep the clock uncertainty as small as possible — which is why Google deploys a GPS receiver or atomic clock in each datacenter, allowing clocks to be synchronized to within about 7 ms
It commits immediately and resolves conflicts later; no special hardware is needed
It waits one second per transaction, using NTP only
It uses logical clocks and no waiting

questions.explanation: A 7 ms commit wait bounds a single sequential committer to roughly 143 commits per second. The chapter notes that clock-based distributed transaction semantics is an area of active research — interesting, but not yet implemented in mainstream databases outside of Google.

questions.question: What problem opens 'Process Pauses', and how does a lease solve it?

options.text: A database with a single leader per partition faces the question: how does a node know that it is still leader — that it hasn't been declared dead by the others — and that it may safely accept writes? One option is for the leader to obtain a lease from the other nodes, which is similar to a lock with a timeout: only one node can hold the lease at any one time, so when a node obtains a lease it knows that it is the leader for some amount of time until the lease expires. To remain leader, the node must periodically renew the lease before it expires; if the node fails it stops renewing the lease, so another node can take over when it expires
The node asks all other nodes on every write; a lease caches the answer
The node checks its own clock; a lease adds a timestamp
There is no problem; leaders are permanent

questions.explanation: A lock with a timeout, renewed while healthy.

questions.question: What is wrong with a request-handling loop that checks whether the lease has less than 10 seconds remaining before renewing?

options.text: It is relying on synchronized clocks: the expiry time on the lease is set by a different machine — perhaps as the current time plus 30 seconds — and it is being compared to the local system clock. If the clocks are out of sync by more than a few seconds, this code will start doing strange things, because it mixes a remote machine's time-of-day clock reading with the local one
It renews too often, wasting network bandwidth
It uses a monotonic clock, which cannot measure expiry
Nothing is wrong with it

questions.explanation: Comparing a remotely-set time-of-day expiry against a local clock is the bug.

questions.question: How long can garbage collection pauses last, and what does the chapter say about 'concurrent' collectors?

options.text: Many programming language runtimes such as the Java Virtual Machine have a garbage collector that occasionally needs to stop all running threads — these stop-the-world GC pauses have sometimes been known to last for several minutes. Even so-called concurrent garbage collectors like the HotSpot JVM's CMS cannot fully run in parallel with the application code: even they need to stop the world from time to time.
