Although the pauses can often be reduced by changing allocation patterns or tuning GC settings, we must assume the worst if we want to offer robust guarantees
GC pauses last at most a few milliseconds; concurrent collectors never stop the world
GC pauses last seconds and can be eliminated by tuning
GC pauses do not affect distributed systems

questions.explanation: Several minutes is an order of magnitude larger than most lease durations.

questions.question: Which whole-machine suspension causes does the chapter describe? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: In virtualized environments a virtual machine can be suspended, pausing the execution of all processes and saving the contents of memory to disk, and resumed — a pause that can occur at any time in a process's execution and can last for an arbitrary length of time
Live migration of virtual machines from one host to another without a reboot, where the length of the pause depends on the rate at which processes are writing to memory
On end-user devices such as laptops, execution may also be suspended and resumed arbitrarily, for example when the user closes the lid of their laptop
Network interface resets, which suspend the CPU

questions.explanation: Three whole-machine causes, all invisible to the paused process.

questions.question: Describe the scheduling-related pauses and define steal time.

options.text: When the operating system context-switches to another thread, or when the hypervisor switches to a different virtual machine, the currently running thread can be paused at any arbitrary point in the code. In the case of a virtual machine, the CPU time spent in other virtual machines is known as steal time. If the machine is under heavy load — if there is a long queue of threads waiting to run — it may take some time before the paused thread gets to run again
Steal time is CPU time consumed by the garbage collector
Steal time is time lost to clock drift
Context switches cannot pause a thread mid-function

questions.explanation: Arbitrary preemption points, with steal time as the virtualized variant.

questions.question: Describe the surprise disk I/O pause cause and its compounding factors.

options.text: If the application performs synchronous disk access, a thread may be paused waiting for a slow disk I/O operation to complete. Disk access can happen surprisingly, even if the code doesn't explicitly mention file access — for example the Java classloader lazily loads class files when they are first used, which could happen at any time in the program execution. I/O pauses and GC pauses may even conspire to combine their delays, and if the disk is actually a network filesystem or network block device such as Amazon's EBS, the I/O latency is further subject to the variability of network delays
Disk I/O only pauses threads that explicitly open files
Disk I/O pauses are bounded by the disk's seek time
Network storage eliminates I/O pauses

questions.explanation: Lazy classloading is the surprising trigger; network storage and GC are the compounding factors.

questions.question: Explain the swapping-related pause and define thrashing.

options.text: If the operating system is configured to allow swapping to disk (paging), a simple memory access may result in a page fault that requires a page from disk to be loaded into memory, and the thread is paused while this slow I/O operation takes place. If memory pressure is high, this may in turn require a different page to be swapped out to disk. In extreme circumstances the operating system may spend most of its time swapping pages in and out of memory and getting little actual work done — known as thrashing. To avoid this, paging is often disabled on server machines, if you would rather kill a process to free up memory than risk thrashing
Thrashing means excessive garbage collection
Thrashing means excessive context switching
Paging never causes pauses on modern systems

questions.explanation: Disabling paging on servers is the standard operational response.

questions.question: Describe the signal-based pause and the general conclusion the chapter draws.

options.text: A Unix process can be paused by sending it the SIGSTOP signal — for example by pressing Ctrl-Z in a shell — which immediately stops the process from getting any more CPU cycles until it is resumed with SIGCONT, at which point it continues running where it left off. Even if your environment does not normally use SIGSTOP, it might be sent accidentally by an operations engineer. All of these occurrences can preempt the running thread at any point and resume it at some later time, without the thread even noticing — similar to making multi-threaded code on a single machine thread-safe, where you can't assume anything about timing because arbitrary context switches and parallelism may occur
SIGSTOP terminates the process permanently
SIGSTOP is only available in virtualized environments
SIGSTOP pauses only I/O, not CPU

questions.explanation: The thread does not notice, which is exactly what makes these pauses dangerous.

questions.question: Why don't single-machine concurrency tools transfer to distributed systems?

options.text: When writing multi-threaded code on a single machine we have fairly good tools for making it thread-safe: mutexes, semaphores, atomic counters, lock-free data structures, blocking queues and so on. Unfortunately these tools don't directly translate to distributed systems, because a distributed system has no shared memory — only messages sent over an unreliable network. A node in a distributed system must assume that its execution can be paused for a significant length of time at any point, even in the middle of a function: during the pause the rest of the world keeps moving and may even declare the paused node dead, and eventually the paused node may continue running without even noticing that it was asleep until it checks its clock sometime later
They transfer directly; distributed locks are the same as mutexes
They fail only because of clock skew
They fail only because of network latency

questions.explanation: No shared memory is the structural reason; unnoticed pauses are the practical one.

questions.question: Define a hard real-time system, and what does the 'Is real-time really real?' box distinguish?

options.text: In embedded systems, real-time means that a system is carefully designed and tested to meet specified timing guarantees in all circumstances — failure to respond within a specified time can cause serious damage, as in aircraft, rockets, robots and cars, which must respond quickly and predictably to sensor inputs. This contrasts with the more vague use of the term real-time on the web, where servers push data to clients and stream processing happens without hard response time constraints. The airbag illustration: you wouldn't want the release of the airbag to be delayed due to an inopportune GC pause in the airbag release system
Real-time means high-performance, and both usages agree
Real-time means low latency, with no timing guarantee
The two usages are identical

questions.explanation: Guaranteed deadlines in all circumstances versus 'fast enough usually'.

questions.question: What does providing real-time guarantees require, and what does it cost? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Support from all levels of the software stack: a real-time operating system that allows processes to be scheduled with a guaranteed allocation of CPU time in specified intervals; library functions must document their worst-case execution times; dynamic memory allocation may be restricted or disallowed entirely (real-time garbage collectors exist, but the application must still ensure it doesn't give the GC too much work to do); and an enormous amount of testing and measurement must be done to ensure guarantees are met
All of this severely restricts the range of programming languages, libraries and tools that can be used, since most languages and tools do not provide real-time guarantees

Developing real-time systems is very expensive, and they are most commonly used in safety-critical embedded devices. Moreover, 'real-time' is not the same as 'high-performance': real-time systems may have lower throughput, since they have to prioritize timely responses above all else

For most server-side data processing systems, real-time guarantees are simply not economical or appropriate — so these systems must suffer the pauses and clock instability that come from operating in a non-real-time environment

questions.explanation: Everything required, and why server-side systems decline to pay for it.

questions.question: Which techniques does the chapter offer for limiting the impact of garbage collection?

options.text: Treat GC pauses like brief planned outages of a node, letting other nodes handle requests from clients while one node is collecting its garbage: the runtime can warn the application that a node soon requires a GC pause, and the application can stop sending new requests to that node, wait for it to finish processing outstanding requests, and then perform the GC while no requests are in progress — hiding GC pauses from clients and reducing the high percentiles of response time, a variant used by some latency-sensitive financial trading systems. A second technique is to use the garbage collector only for short-lived objects, which are fast to collect, and to restart processes periodically before they accumulate enough long-lived objects to require a full GC of long-lived objects — with one node restarted at a time, and traffic shifted away before the planned restart, like a rolling upgrade
Disable garbage collection entirely
Use a real-time operating system for all server workloads
Increase the heap size until GC never runs

questions.explanation: Both emerging ideas rely on the runtime tracking the rate of object allocation and the remaining free memory over time so collections can be scheduled. The caveat: these measures cannot fully prevent garbage collection pauses, only reduce their impact on the application.

questions.question: Summarize how distributed systems differ from a single computer, and the limit on a node's knowledge.

options.text: There is no shared memory, only message passing via an unreliable network with variable delays, and the system may suffer from partial failures, unreliable clocks and processing pauses. Consequently a node in the network cannot know anything for sure — it can only make guesses based on the messages it receives or doesn't receive. A node can only find out what state another node is in by exchanging messages with it, and if a remote node doesn't respond there is no way of knowing what state it is in, because problems in the network cannot reliably be distinguished from problems at a node
Nodes share memory but not clocks, so only timing is uncertain
Nodes can determine each other's state by direct inspection
Only partial failure distinguishes distributed systems

questions.explanation: The chapter admits these discussions border on the philosophical, since our mechanisms for perception and measurement are unreliable — though in computing, unlike philosophy, we do expect the system to obey the laws we expect of the physical world, such as cause and effect.

questions.question: How does the chapter say we avoid 'figuring out the meaning of life'?

options.text: It is possible to state the assumptions we are making about the behavior — the system model — and design the actual system in such a way that it meets those assumptions. Algorithms can be proved to function correctly within a certain system model, which means that reliable behavior is achievable even if the underlying system model provides very few guarantees. The honest qualifier: although it is possible to make software well behaved in an unreliable system model, it is not straightforward to do so
By assuming the network is reliable and testing thoroughly
By using only single-node systems
By accepting that reliable behavior is unachievable

questions.explanation: State the model, design to it, prove within it.

questions.question: Describe the three funeral scenarios in 'The Truth Is Defined by the Majority'.

options.text: First, the asymmetric fault: a node can receive all messages sent to it, but any outgoing messages from that node are dropped or delayed — so even though the node is working perfectly well, other nodes cannot hear its responses and eventually declare it dead. The node is dragged to the graveyard kicking and screaming 'I'm not dead!', but since nobody can hear its screaming, the funeral procession continues with stoic determination. Second, the self-aware version: the node may notice that the messages it is sending are not being acknowledged and realize that there must be a fault in the network, but it is nevertheless wrongly declared dead by the other nodes and cannot do anything about it. Third, the GC pause: a node is preempted by the garbage collector and paused for one minute; during this time all requests time out and other nodes load it onto the hearse — then the supposedly dead node suddenly raises its head out of the coffin in full health and starts speaking, doesn't even realize that an entire minute has passed, since from its perspective hardly any time has passed
Three scenarios about clock skew, network loss and disk corruption
Three scenarios about leader election, failover and split brain
Three scenarios about Byzantine nodes lying to each other

questions.explanation: The moral: a node cannot necessarily trust its own judgment of a situation, so a distributed system cannot exclusively rely on a single node — otherwise, if that node fails, the system would be stuck and unable to recover.

questions.question: Which examples of 'only one of some thing' does the chapter give? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Only one node is allowed to be the leader for a database partition, to avoid split brain
Only one transaction or client is allowed to hold the lock for a particular resource or object, to prevent concurrently writing to it and corrupting it
Only one user is allowed to register a particular username, because a username must uniquely identify a user
Only one node is allowed to hold a clock reading

questions.explanation: The trap: even if a node believes that it is 'the chosen one', that doesn't necessarily mean a quorum of nodes agrees. A node may have formerly been the leader, but if the other nodes declared it dead in the meantime due to a network interruption or GC pause, it may have been demoted and another leader may already have been elected — yet if it keeps acting as the chosen one and other nodes believe it, the system as a whole may do something incorrect.

questions.question: Walk through Figure 8-4, and which real system had this bug?

options.text: A file in a storage service can only be accessed by one client at a time, because if multiple clients tried to write to it the file would become corrupted — so each client must obtain a lease from a lock service before accessing the file. But if the client holding the lease is paused for too long, its lease expires; another client can obtain a lease for the same file and start writing; and then when the paused client comes back it believes, incorrectly, that it still has a valid lease and proceeds to also write to the file — so the clients' writes clash and corrupt the file. The bug is not theoretical: HBase used to have this problem
Two nodes both claim leadership and diverge; Cassandra had this bug
A clock jumps backward and writes are reordered; Riak had this bug
A network partition splits the cluster; ZooKeeper had this bug

questions.explanation: The figure's caption: incorrect implementation of a distributed lock, where client 1 believes that it still has a valid lease, even though it has expired, and thus corrupts a file in storage.

questions.question: Define a fencing token and walk through Figure 8-5 with its token numbers.

options.text: Fencing ensures that a node under a false belief of being 'the chosen one' cannot disrupt the rest of the system: every time the lock server grants a lock or lease, it also returns a fencing token — a number that increases every time a lock is granted — and every time a client sends a write request to the storage service it must include its current fencing token. In Figure 8-5, client 1 acquires the lease with a token of 33 but then goes into a long pause and the lease expires; client 2 acquires the lease with a token of 34 and sends a write request including token 34; later client 1 comes back to life and sends its write including its token value 33, but the storage server remembers that it has already processed a write with a higher token number (34), and so it rejects the request with token 33
A fencing token is a timestamp; the server rejects older timestamps
A fencing token is a client ID; the server accepts only the newest client
A fencing token is a checksum of the write

questions.explanation: The caption: making access to storage safe by allowing writes only in the order of increasing fencing tokens.

questions.question: Which ZooKeeper values can serve as fencing tokens, and where must the check happen?

options.text: The transaction ID zxid or the node version cversion, both of which are guaranteed to be monotonically increasing. The check must happen at the resource itself: the resource must take an active role in checking tokens by rejecting any writes with an older token than one that has already been processed — it is not sufficient to rely on clients checking their lock status themselves. For resources that do not explicitly support fencing tokens you may still be able to work around the limitation, for example with a file storage service you could include the fencing token in the filename. Server-side checking is arguably a good thing: it is unwise for a service to assume that its clients will always be well behaved, because the clients are often run by people whose priorities are very different from the priorities of the people running the service, so it's a good idea for any service to protect itself from accidentally abusive clients
The session ID and the ephemeral node path; the client must check
The server timestamp and the watch counter; the lock service must check
ZooKeeper does not provide suitable tokens

questions.explanation: Some kind of check is necessary to avoid processing requests outside of the lock's protection, and the resource is the only place it can be enforced.

questions.question: What can fencing tokens not defend against, and what is the book's assumption about nodes?

options.text: Fencing tokens can detect and block a node that is inadvertently acting in error — for example because it hasn't yet found out that its lease has expired — but if the node deliberately wanted to subvert the system's guarantees, it could easily do so by sending messages with a fake fencing token. The book assumes nodes are unreliable but honest: they may be slow or never respond, and their state may be outdated, but if a node does respond it is telling the 'truth' — to the best of its knowledge it is playing by the rules of the protocol. Distributed systems problems become much harder if there is a risk that nodes may 'lie' — send arbitrary faulty or corrupted responses, or claim to have received a particular message when in fact it didn't — which is known as a Byzantine fault
Fencing tokens defend against all faults including malice
Fencing tokens defend only against clock skew
The book assumes nodes are adversarial by default

questions.explanation: Reaching consensus in this untrusting environment is known as the Byzantine Generals Problem.

questions.question: Describe the Two Generals Problem.

options.text: Two army generals need to agree on a battle plan, but having set up camp on two different sites they can only communicate by messenger — and the messengers sometimes get delayed or lost, like packets in a network. The Byzantine Generals Problem generalizes it, and consensus is discussed in Chapter 9
Two generals must agree despite one of them being a traitor
Two generals share a radio channel that may be jammed
Two generals must synchronize their clocks

questions.explanation: Lost and delayed messengers, with no traitors — that is the non-Byzantine version.

questions.question: How does the Byzantine version differ?

options.text: There are n generals who need to agree, and their endeavor is hampered by the fact that there are some traitors in their midst. Most of the generals are loyal and send truthful messages, but the traitors may try to deceive and confuse the others by sending fake or untrue messages while trying to remain undiscovered — and crucially, it is not known in advance who the traitors are
There are exactly three generals, one of whom is known to be a traitor
All generals are traitors
The messengers are traitors rather than the generals

questions.explanation: Unknown identity of the traitors is what makes the problem hard.

questions.question: Where does the name 'Byzantine' come from?

options.text: Byzantium was an ancient Greek city that later became Constantinople, in the place which is now Istanbul in Turkey. There isn't any historic evidence that the generals of Byzantium were any more prone to intrigue and conspiracy than those elsewhere: rather, the name is derived from Byzantine in the sense of excessively complicated, bureaucratic, devious — a sense used in politics long before computers. Lamport wanted to choose a nationality that would not offend any readers, and he was advised that calling it The Albanian Generals Problem was not such a good idea
It refers to documented treachery among Byzantine generals
It refers to the Byzantine Empire's cryptographic systems
It was coined by Kyle Kingsbury

questions.explanation: The adjective, not the history, is the source.

questions.question: Define Byzantine fault-tolerant.

options.text: A system is Byzantine fault-tolerant if it continues to operate correctly even if some of the nodes are malfunctioning and not obeying the protocol, or if malicious attackers are interfering with the network
If it tolerates only malicious attackers, not malfunctioning nodes
If it tolerates only malfunctioning nodes, not attackers
If it tolerates network partitions

questions.explanation: Note both halves: the nodes need not be adversarial to be Byzantine — merely arbitrary.

questions.question: Why must flight control systems tolerate Byzantine faults?

options.text: In aerospace environments the data in a computer's memory or CPU register could become corrupted by radiation, leading it to respond to other nodes in arbitrarily unpredictable ways. Since a system failure would be very expensive — an aircraft crashing and killing everyone on board, or a rocket colliding with the International Space Station — flight control systems must tolerate Byzantine faults
Because pilots may issue malicious commands
Because flight software is written by untrusted vendors
Because air traffic networks are public

questions.explanation: Physics, not malice, produces arbitrary behaviour here.

questions.question: What is the second circumstance where Byzantine fault tolerance is relevant?

options.text: In a system with multiple participating organizations, some participants may attempt to cheat or defraud others — in such circumstances it is not safe for a node to simply trust another node's messages, since they may be sent with malicious intent. For example peer-to-peer networks like Bitcoin and other blockchains can be considered a way of getting mutually untrusting parties to agree whether a transaction happened or not, without relying on a central authority
In single-organization datacenters, where insiders may be malicious
In web applications, where browsers are untrusted
In embedded systems, where hardware may be counterfeit

questions.explanation: Absence of a central authority among mutually untrusting parties is the defining condition.

questions.question: Why does this book assume no Byzantine faults? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Trust boundary: in your datacenter, all the nodes are controlled by your organization, so they can hopefully be trusted
Physics: radiation levels are low enough that memory corruption is not a major problem
Complexity: protocols for making systems Byzantine fault-tolerant are quite complicated, and fault-tolerant embedded systems rely on support from the hardware level
Cost: in most server-side data systems the cost of deploying Byzantine fault-tolerant solutions makes them impractical

questions.explanation: Four reasons: trust, physics, complexity and cost.

questions.question: Which party must web applications expect arbitrary behaviour from, and what do they use instead of a Byzantine fault-tolerant protocol?

options.text: Clients that are under end-user control, such as web browsers — which is why input validation, sanitization and output escaping are so important, for example to prevent SQL injection and cross-site scripting. But we typically don't use Byzantine fault-tolerant protocols here: instead we simply make the server the authority on deciding what client behavior is and isn't allowed. In peer-to-peer networks, where there is no such central authority, Byzantine fault tolerance is more relevant
Other servers in the same datacenter; they use Byzantine consensus
Database replicas; they use quorum voting
Network switches; they use checksums

questions.explanation: A central authority replaces Byzantine agreement whenever one exists.

questions.question: Why can't a Byzantine fault-tolerant algorithm save you from your own bugs?

options.text: A bug in the software could be regarded as a Byzantine fault, but if you deploy the same software to all nodes, then a Byzantine fault-tolerant algorithm cannot save you, since most such algorithms require a supermajority of more than two-thirds of the nodes to be functioning correctly — with four nodes, at most one may malfunction. To use this approach against bugs you would have to have four independent implementations of the same software and hope that a bug only appears in one of the four implementations
Because bugs are not Byzantine faults by definition
Because BFT algorithms require unanimity
It can save you, provided the bug is rare

questions.explanation: With n = 4, more than two-thirds means more than 2.67 nodes correct, so at least 3 correct and therefore at most 1 faulty — and the same bug in the same code breaks all four.

questions.question: Could a protocol protect against vulnerabilities and compromise?

options.text: It would be appealing, but unfortunately this is not realistic either: in most systems, if an attacker can compromise one node they can probably compromise all of them, because they are probably running the same software. Thus traditional mechanisms — authentication, access control, encryption, firewalls and so on — continue to be the main protection against attackers
Yes, Byzantine fault tolerance solves security completely
Yes, provided fewer than one-third of nodes are compromised
No, and no protection is possible

questions.explanation: Homogeneity of software defeats the quorum assumption for attackers as well as for bugs.

questions.question: What does the chapter mean by weak forms of lying, and how does it characterize the countermeasures?

options.text: Although we assume that nodes are generally honest, it can be worth adding mechanisms to software that guard against weak forms of 'lying' — for example invalid messages due to hardware issues, software bugs and misconfiguration. Such protection mechanisms are not full-blown Byzantine fault tolerance, as they would not withstand a determined adversary, but they are nevertheless simple and pragmatic steps toward better reliability
They constitute full Byzantine fault tolerance at low cost
They defend against determined adversaries
They are not worth implementing

questions.explanation: Pragmatic partial protection, honestly labelled as such.

questions.question: What does the chapter recommend about packet corruption?

options.text: Network packets do sometimes get corrupted due to hardware issues or bugs in operating systems, drivers, routers and so on. Usually corrupted packets are caught by the checksums built into TCP and UDP, but sometimes they evade detection — so simple measures are usually sufficient protection against such corruption, such as checksums in the application-level protocol
TCP checksums are sufficient; no application-level check is needed
Full cryptographic signing is required on every packet
Packet corruption does not occur in modern networks

questions.explanation: Application-level checksums catch what TCP and UDP miss.

questions.question: What input checks does the chapter name, inside and outside the firewall?

options.text: A publicly accessible application must carefully sanitize any inputs from users — for example checking that a value is within a reasonable range and limiting the size of strings to prevent denial of service through large memory allocations. An internal service behind a firewall may be able to get away with less strict checks on inputs, but some basic sanity-checking of values, for example in protocol parsing, is a good idea
Public applications need no checks; internal ones need strict checks
Both need identical, maximally strict checks
Neither needs checks if TLS is used

questions.explanation: Graduated strictness by trust boundary, but never zero.

questions.question: Describe NTP's majority check and the conclusion.

options.text: An NTP client can be configured with multiple server addresses: when synchronizing, the client contacts all of them, estimates their errors, and checks that a majority of servers agree on some time range. As long as most of the servers are okay, a misconfigured NTP server that is reporting an incorrect time is detected as an outlier and is excluded from synchronization — so the use of multiple servers makes NTP more robust than if it only uses a single server
The client uses only the first responding server
The client averages all servers including outliers
The client trusts the server with the lowest stratum number unconditionally

questions.explanation: This is the majority-agreement idea from The Truth Is Defined by the Majority, applied to time.

questions.question: Define a system model, and why do algorithms need one?

options.text: Algorithms need to be written in a way that does not depend too heavily on the details of the hardware and software configuration on which they are run, which requires us to somehow formalize the kinds of faults that we expect to happen in a system. We do this by defining a system model, which is an abstraction that describes what things an algorithm may assume
A system model is a performance benchmark
A system model is a deployment topology diagram
A system model is the implementation of an algorithm

questions.explanation: Formalizing expected faults is what allows correctness proofs — needed for problems like consensus in Chapter 9.

questions.question: State the synchronous model, the misreading it heads off, and the verdict on its realism.

options.text: It assumes bounded network delay, bounded process pauses, and bounded clock error. This does not imply exactly synchronized clocks or zero network delay; it simply means you know that network delay, pauses, and clock drift will never exceed some fixed upper bound. The verdict: the synchronous model is not a realistic model of most practical systems, because unbounded delays and pauses do occur
It assumes zero delay and perfectly synchronized clocks, and is realistic
It assumes unbounded delay, and is realistic
It assumes no clocks at all

questions.explanation: Bounded, not zero — and still unrealistic.

questions.question: Define partial synchrony and give both halves of the argument for its realism.

options.text: Partial synchrony means that a system behaves like a synchronous system most of the time, but sometimes exceeds the bounds for network delay, process pauses and clock drift. This is a realistic model of many systems: most of the time networks and processes are quite well behaved — otherwise we would never be able to get anything done — but we have to reckon with the fact that any timing assumptions may be shattered occasionally, and when that happens network delay, pauses and clock error may become arbitrarily large
It means delays are always large but bounded
It means clocks are synchronized but networks are not
It is not a realistic model

questions.explanation: Note 'arbitrarily large', not 'large but bounded' — that distinction is what makes the model hard.

questions.question: What is an algorithm forbidden from doing in the asynchronous model?

options.text: It is not allowed to make any timing assumptions — in fact it does not even have a clock, so it cannot use timeouts. Some algorithms can be designed for the asynchronous model, but it is very restrictive
It cannot send messages, only receive them
It cannot use persistent storage
It cannot assume nodes are honest

questions.explanation: No clock means no timeouts, which rules out most practical failure detection.

questions.question: Match the timing models to their defining statements.

options.text: Synchronous: network delay, process pauses and clock error all have a known fixed upper bound. Partially synchronous: behaves as though bounded most of the time, but occasionally the bounds are exceeded and delay, pauses and clock error may become arbitrarily large. Asynchronous: no timing assumptions at all, not even a clock, so no timeouts
Synchronous has no clock; asynchronous has bounded delay
Partially synchronous has no clock; synchronous is occasionally unbounded
All three assume bounded delay, differing only in clock accuracy

questions.explanation: The chapter calls the synchronous model not realistic, partial synchrony a realistic model of many systems, and the asynchronous model very restrictive.

questions.question: State the crash-stop assumption, including what makes it stop rather than merely crash.

options.text: In the crash-stop model, an algorithm may assume that a node can fail in only one way, namely by crashing: the node may suddenly stop responding at any moment, and thereafter that node is gone forever — it never comes back
The node crashes and recovers after a known delay
The node crashes and recovers with its memory intact
The node slows down but never stops

questions.explanation: 'Never comes back' is what distinguishes crash-stop from crash-recovery.

questions.question: Give the crash-recovery assumptions, being precise about state.

options.text: Nodes may crash at any moment, and perhaps start responding again after some unknown time. In the crash-recovery model, nodes are assumed to have stable storage — nonvolatile disk storage — that is preserved across crashes, while the in-memory state is assumed to be lost
In-memory state survives; disk state is lost
Both in-memory and disk state survive
Both are lost, and recovery time is known in advance

questions.explanation: Disk survives, memory does not, and the recovery time is unknown.

questions.question: State the Byzantine node model, and why does 'arbitrary' matter?

options.text: Nodes may do absolutely anything, including trying to trick and deceive other nodes. The parenthetical 'arbitrary' matters because the model does not require malice: as the radiation-corrupted register example showed, arbitrary behavior can be produced by physics alone, so a node need not be adversarial to be Byzantine
Nodes are always adversarial and controlled by an attacker
Nodes may only crash or slow down
Nodes may lie only about timing

questions.explanation: Arbitrary covers both malice and mere corruption.

questions.question: Of the nine combinations of timing and node models, which does the chapter single out?

options.text: The partially synchronous model with crash-recovery faults is generally the most useful model — which immediately raises the question: how do distributed algorithms cope with that model?
The synchronous model with crash-stop faults
The asynchronous model with Byzantine faults
The synchronous model with Byzantine faults

questions.explanation: Realistic timing plus realistic recovery behaviour, which is exactly what Chapter 9's algorithms target.
